patient.chief_complaint: Bilateral ptosis, dysarthria, and dysphagia worse in afternoons — also has chronic skin rash
patient.hpi:
A 69-year-old Indian man with a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and a chronic violaceous pruritic skin eruption on the extremities (diagnosed one year earlier as lichen planus by dermatology) presented to the neurology ward with a 20-day history of mild bilateral ptosis, dysarthria, and progressive dysphagia. Dysarthria developed first — a nasal quality to his speech that his wife noticed was more pronounced by evening — followed within 3 days by difficulty swallowing solids that progressed over the next week to difficulty with liquids. He noted that symptoms were consistently and markedly better in the morning upon waking and significantly worsened through the afternoon and evening. He denied diplopia, headache, vertigo, dizziness, shortness of breath, or limb weakness.

He had no recent infections, travel, or significant dietary changes. His family history was unremarkable for neuromuscular disease. On physical examination, he was afebrile with normal vital signs. Dermatologic examination confirmed flat-topped violaceous papules on the flexural surfaces of both lower extremities with overlying hyperpigmented macules — characteristic lichen planus morphology. Neurological examination demonstrated asymmetric bilateral ptosis (left greater than right) without ophthalmoplegia. Gag reflex was severely reduced. Palate elevation was symmetric but weak. Tongue movements were intact with no fasciculations or atrophy. Proximal muscle strength was 5/5 with clinically apparent fatigability on sustained resistance testing. Reflexes were 2+ symmetric. Sensation was intact throughout.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: AChR antibody-positive generalized myasthenia gravis, late-onset, with concurrent lichen planus (autoimmune background)

differential.key_features: Age and hypertension raise concern; MRI without acute lesion; fluctuating fatigable pattern incompatible.
T2DM; cranial mononeuropathy is acute, monocular, painful.
No baseline CMAP reduction; no facilitation; AChR positive.
Patient not on penicillamine or implicated agents.
No tongue fasciculations or atrophy; SFEMG/RNS will discriminate.

optimal_actions.action: Order serologies: anti-AChR (binding, blocking, modulating), anti-MuSK, anti-LRP4, and TSH/free-T4 for thyroid autoimmunity
optimal_actions.expected_finding: AChR antibody positive; TSH evaluates for comorbid thyroid disease

optimal_actions.action: Order repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) at 2-3 Hz across proximal and facial muscles
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Decrement >10% in symptomatic muscles supports postsynaptic NMJ disorder
Increased jitter and blocking on extensor digitorum communis or orbicularis oculi confirms NMJ transmission failure

optimal_actions.action: Order CT chest with contrast for thymoma screening
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No thymoma; thymic involution appropriate for age

optimal_actions.action: Review MGFA classification and current treatment guidance (pyridostigmine, prednisone, steroid-sparing, IVIG/PLEX, thymectomy)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: MGFA classification stages disease severity; thymectomy benefits AChR+ generalized MG (MGTX); IVIG/PLEX for crisis

tool_parameters.query: myasthenia gravis MGFA classification treatment thymectomy

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions for MG-exacerbating agents (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, neuromuscular blockers, procainamide)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Flag aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, IV magnesium, telithromycin, NMBs as contraindicated or use-with-caution in MG

optimal_actions.action: Bedside respiratory function testing (FVC, MIP/MEP, NIF) — repeat q4h in crisis
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Baseline FVC/NIF to assess crisis risk in patients with bulbar or limb involvement

optimal_actions.action: Bedside ice-pack test for ptosis (cheap, ~80% sensitive for ocular MG)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Improvement of ptosis after 2 minutes of cooling supports MG

useless_tools.rationale: MG is a peripheral neuromuscular junction disorder; EEG has no diagnostic role.
No CSF role in MG; LP risks complications without diagnostic yield.
Advanced imaging (PET/MR spectroscopy/perfusion) is not indicated for MG diagnosis or staging; CT chest covers thymoma screening.
Echocardiography is not indicated for MG unless a comorbid cardiac question exists.
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated for MG unless arrhythmia or autonomic disease is independently suspected.

sequence_constraints.reason: Order AChR/MuSK/LRP4 serologies first; reserve single-fiber EMG for seronegative or RNS-non-diagnostic cases (resource stewardship).

critical_actions: RNS — clearly abnormal 14-16% decrement here supports diagnosis
Initiate pyridostigmine and coordinate diabetes management for steroid plan
Dermatology continued care for lichen planus
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT prescribe aminoglycoside antibiotics (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) — risk of precipitating myasthenic crisis
Do NOT prescribe fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) — FDA black-box warning for MG exacerbation
Do NOT prescribe telithromycin — contraindicated in MG
Do NOT administer IV magnesium for MG patients (e.g., for hypomagnesaemia, eclampsia prophylaxis) without alternative — blocks NMJ transmission
Do NOT use non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers without anaesthesia/MG-aware dosing protocols
Do NOT initiate high-dose corticosteroids as sole outpatient therapy without hospitalization or pyridostigmine bridge — risk of paradoxical worsening at days 5-10
Do NOT attribute fluctuating fatigable weakness to a functional disorder before completing serology + RNS + single-fiber EMG workup
key_reasoning_points: Fluctuating, fatigable weakness with diurnal pattern (worse evening) is the clinical hallmark of MG — fixed weakness suggests an alternative diagnosis.
Ocular involvement (ptosis, diplopia) is asymmetric and fatigable in MG; thyroid eye disease causes restrictive (not fatigable) ophthalmoplegia.
Single-fiber EMG (sensitivity >95%) is the most sensitive electrodiagnostic test — order when RNS is non-diagnostic or serology is negative.
All confirmed MG cases require CT chest for thymoma — present in roughly 10-15% of generalized MG; thymectomy (MGTX trial) improves long-term outcomes in non-thymoma AChR+ MG as well.
Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, and neuromuscular blockers can precipitate myasthenic crisis and must be screened against any new prescription.
Lichen planus is an autoimmune skin condition; polyautoimmunity supports MG diagnosis.

red_herrings.data_point: Lichen planus on skin exam — considered as possible paraneoplastic or connective tissue disorder
red_herrings.intended_effect: Lichen planus with bulbar dysfunction might suggest a paraneoplastic process or SLE with neurological involvement
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Lichen planus is an incidental autoimmune co-diagnosis; does not cause bulbar dysfunction; MG is the independent cause

red_herrings.intended_effect: Elevated ESR with neurological symptoms could suggest vasculitis or inflammatory condition
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Non-specific mild elevation; normal CRP; no other vasculitis features; attributed to mild chronic inflammation from lichen planus

red_herrings.data_point: Elevated HbA1c suggesting inadequately controlled diabetes
red_herrings.intended_effect: Poorly controlled diabetes with peripheral neuropathy could cause mild bulbar dysfunction
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Normal nerve conduction on EMG study; T2DM at this HbA1c level would not cause fatigable bulbar weakness; RNS and AChR antibody confirm MG

findings.description:
REPETITIVE NERVE STIMULATION STUDY

Indication: Fatigable ptosis, bulbar dysfunction; RNS for NMJ assessment

TECHNIQUE: 3 Hz RNS performed at anconeus (radial nerve), trapezius (accessory nerve), and orbicularis oculi (facial nerve)

RESULTS:
  Anconeus: Decrement 14% from 1st to 4th stimulus [>10% abnormal] ABNORMAL
  Trapezius: Decrement 16% ABNORMAL
  Orbicularis oculi: Decrement 12% ABNORMAL

MOTOR NERVE CONDUCTION: Normal distal latencies and amplitudes; no evidence of peripheral neuropathy.

SENSORY NERVE CONDUCTION: Normal.

NEEDLE EMG (distal and proximal muscles): Normal insertional activity; no fibrillations, no fasciculations; no myopathic or neuropathic motor unit morphology changes.

HIGH-RATE RNS (50 Hz): No pathological facilitating response.

IMPRESSION: Abnormal decremental responses at 3 Hz in three muscle groups (anconeus 14%, trapezius 16%, orbicularis 12%). Normal needle EMG and nerve conduction. No 50 Hz increment. Findings are consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission. Clinical correlation recommended.

specialized_test.impression: RNS: 14–16% decrement at anconeus, trapezius, orbicularis; normal needle EMG; no 50 Hz increment — decremental pattern consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission

output.interpretation: AChR binding antibody markedly elevated at 11.2 nmol/L (reference < 0.4 nmol/L). AChR blocking antibody positive. Anti-MuSK antibody negative. Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies are found in a subset of patients with neuromuscular junction disorders; an elevated result is associated with autoimmune neuromuscular junction disease
abnormal_values_summary: AChR binding antibody 11.2 nmol/L (ref <0.4 nmol/L) — markedly elevated

findings.description:

MCD: 58 µs [normal <35 µs] MARKEDLY ABNORMAL
Blocking: 20% of potential pairs

IMPRESSION: Markedly increased mean consecutive difference with 20% blocking, consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission. Clinical correlation recommended.

results.title: Clinical literature
results.content:
LITERATURE SEARCH: Lichen Planus and Myasthenia Gravis Association

KEY FINDINGS:
1. POLYAUTOIMMUNE ASSOCIATIONS: Lichen planus is a T-cell–mediated immune disorder; it has been described in association with other autoimmune conditions including neuromuscular junction disease, autoimmune hepatitis, and thyroid disease.
2. CASE SERIES: Small series report co-occurrence of lichen planus and autoimmune neuromuscular disease, suggesting shared immunological susceptibility (HLA-DR1, HLA-DQ1).
3. CLINICAL IMPLICATION: Lichen planus is not known to cause neuromuscular junction dysfunction; the two conditions may share an autoimmune predisposition.
4. STEROIDS: Prednisone is used for both conditions as an immunosuppressive agent.

output.summary: Lichen planus and autoimmune neuromuscular junction disease share a polyautoimmune predisposition; prednisone is used for both conditions.

interactions:
DRUG INTERACTION REVIEW — METFORMIN AND PYRIDOSTIGMINE; PREDNISONE AND METFORMIN

Query: Drug interactions when adding pyridostigmine and prednisone to metformin regimen

FINDINGS:
  METFORMIN + PYRIDOSTIGMINE: No clinically significant pharmacokinetic interaction identified.
  PREDNISONE + METFORMIN: Corticosteroids antagonize insulin action and cause dose-dependent hyperglycemia; blood glucose monitoring should be intensified when adding corticosteroids to existing antidiabetic therapy.
  PREDNISONE (GI): Concurrent NSAID or aspirin use increases GI mucosal irritation risk; gastroprotection recommended.
  AMLODIPINE: At standard doses, amlodipine has a low reported risk of NMJ effects; clinical monitoring is appropriate.
warnings: Prednisone will increase blood glucose — intensify monitoring in diabetic patients; no clinically significant metformin–pyridostigmine interaction.
